en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.1 Chapter on the Performance of Deeds (Kammakaraṇavagga) (AN 2.1.1, PTS AN i 47) “Monks, there are these two kinds of deeds that have been performed and accumulated by a person. What two? There is the deed that leads to one’s own affliction, but not to the affliction of others; and there is the deed that leads to the affliction of others, but not to one’s own affliction. These, monks, are the two kinds of deeds that have been performed and accumulated by a person.”
1. The Discourse on Faults (Vajjasutta).
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, there are these two faults. Which two?
Faults pertaining to the present life and faults pertaining to future lives.
And what, bhikkhus, is the fault pertaining to the present life?
Here, bhikkhus, someone sees that kings, having seized a thief or a wrongdoer, inflict various punishments upon them.
Even when they are being beaten with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with split bamboo;
even when their hands are cut off, their feet are cut off, both hands and feet are cut off, their ears are cut off, their noses are cut off, both ears and noses are cut off;
even when they are subjected to the "spit-roasting" torture, the "conch-shell-shaving" torture, or the "Rāhu’s mouth" torture.
Some perform the "garland of light" penance; some perform the "hand-torch" penance; some perform the "eraka-grass twist" penance; some perform the "bark-cloth" penance;
some perform the "eneyyaka-deer skin" penance; some perform the "fish-hook" penance; some perform the "kahāpaṇa-coin" penance;
some perform the "caustic-lime scarification" penance; some perform the "bar-turning" penance; and some perform the "straw-mat" penance.
While they were doing so— drenching him with boiling oil, having him devoured by dogs, impaling him alive on a stake,
and cutting off his head with a sword—
he thought to himself:
“Indeed, for the sake of such evil deeds, kings seize a thief who has committed a crime and inflict various punishments upon him:
they flog him with whips, they flog him with canes, they flog him with clubs;
they cut off his hand, they cut off his foot, they cut off both his hands and feet; they cut off his ear, they cut off his nose.”

They cut off their ears, they subject them to the *bilaṅgathālika* (the spit-roasting), they subject them to the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* (the conch-shell shaving), they subject them to the *rāhumukha* (the Rāhu-mouth), they subject them to the *jotimālika* (the garland of fire),
they subject them to the *hatthapajjotika* (the torch in the hand), they subject them to the *erakavattika* (the eraka-grass whirling), they subject them to the *cīrakavāsika* (the bark-garment),
they subject them to the *eṇeyyaka* (the antelope-skin), they subject them to the *baḷisamaṁsika* (the meat-hook), and they subject them to the *kahāpaṇika* (the coin-marking).
They subject them to the *khārāpatacchika* torture; they subject them to the *palighaparivattika* torture; they subject them to the *palālapīṭhaka* torture;
they pour boiling oil over them; they have them devoured by dogs; they impale them alive on stakes;
and they cut off their heads with swords.
‘If I were to commit such an evil deed, kings would seize me and subject me to various forms of punishment:
they might flog me with whips... [and so on] ...or they might cut off my head with a sword.
Fearing the blame pertaining to this present life, he does not wander about plundering the property of others.
This, monks, is called the fault pertaining to the present life.
And what, monks, is the fault pertaining to the future life?
Here, monks, a certain person reflects thus:

“Indeed, misconduct of body has a bad, painful result in the future life; misconduct of speech has a bad, painful result in the future life; misconduct of mind has a bad, painful result in the future life.

If I were to engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, why should I not—upon the breakup of the body, after death—reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell?”
Thus, fearing a fault pertaining to the future life, he abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct;
he abandons verbal misconduct and develops verbal good conduct; he abandons mental misconduct and develops mental good conduct; he maintains himself in purity.
This, monks, is called a fault pertaining to the future life.
“Monks, these are the two kinds of faults.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall fear the fault pertaining to the present life; we shall fear the fault pertaining to future lives; we shall be fearful of faults, seeing the danger in faults.’”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
For those who fear wrongdoing and see danger in wrongdoing, it is to be expected that they will be liberated from all wrongdoing. Thus was the first [sutta].
The Discourse on Exertion:
“Monks, these two kinds of exertion are difficult to achieve in the world.”
Which two?
The striving of householders living at home for the purpose of providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
and the striving of those who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness for the purpose of relinquishing all acquisitions.
“Monks, these two kinds of striving are difficult to accomplish in the world.
Of these two kinds of striving, monks, the foremost is that which aims at the relinquishing of all acquisitions.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:”
‘We shall exert effort for the sake of relinquishing all acquisitions.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. This is the second [discourse].
The Discourse on What Causes Torment:
"Bhikkhus, these two things cause torment."
Which two?
Here, monks, for a certain person, misconduct of body has been committed, while good conduct of body has not been practiced;
misconduct of speech has been committed, while good conduct of speech has not been practiced.
Mental misconduct has been committed, and mental good conduct has not been practiced.
He is tormented by the thought, "I have committed bodily misconduct," and he is tormented by the thought, "I have failed to practice bodily good conduct";
he is tormented by the thought, "I have committed verbal misconduct," and he is tormented by the thought, "I have failed to practice verbal good conduct."
“I have committed a mental misconduct,” he is tormented; “I have failed to perform a mental good deed,” he is tormented.
These, monks, are the two things that cause torment. Thus ends the third [discourse].
The Discourse on What is Not Tormenting:
“Bhikkhus, these two things are not tormenting.”
Which two?
Here, monks, for a certain person, good conduct of body has been performed and misconduct of body has not been performed;
good conduct of speech has been performed and misconduct of speech has not been performed.
Good conduct of mind has been performed, and misconduct of mind has not been performed.
He does not burn with remorse thinking, "Good conduct of body has been performed by me," nor does he burn thinking, "Misconduct of body has not been performed by me";
he does not burn thinking, "Good conduct of speech has been performed by me," nor does he burn thinking, "Misconduct of speech has not been performed by me."
“I have performed good conduct with the mind,” he does not feel remorse; “I have not performed misconduct with the mind,” he does not feel remorse.
These, monks, are the two things that do not cause remorse. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].
Upaññātasutta “Bhikkhus, I have proclaimed two things:”
There is both dissatisfaction with wholesome states and non-desistance in striving.
Indeed, monks, I strove without desisting:
"Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood dry up in my body, [yet I shall not desist from my exertion until I have attained what is beyond the human]."
‘That which is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion—until that is reached, there shall be no cessation of my effort.
Monks, through diligence I have attained enlightenment; through diligence I have attained the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Even if you, monks, were to strive with unwavering persistence, thinking:
"Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood dry up in the body;
rather than failing to attain that which can be reached by human strength, human energy, and human exertion, I shall not relax my vigor," [you would surely reach it].

‘...the shape will be. Monks, before long you too, having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life—for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—will dwell having entered upon it.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall strive without turning back.
Even if only skin, sinew, and bone remain, and the flesh and blood of our bodies dry up,
we will not cease our effort until we have attained that which can be attained by human strength, human vigor, and human perseverance.’
‘There will be its shape.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
The fifth.
Saṁyojanasutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these two things.
Which two?
That which is the contemplation of gratification in phenomena that lead to fetters, and that which is the contemplation of disenchantment in phenomena that lead to fetters.
Monks, one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that lead to fetters does not abandon lust, does not abandon hatred, and does not abandon delusion.
"Without abandoning lust, without abandoning hatred, and without abandoning delusion, one is not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
One is not liberated from suffering, I say.
By dwelling contemplating revulsion toward phenomena that fetter, monks, one abandons lust, abandons hatred, and abandons delusion."
"Having abandoned lust, having abandoned hatred, having abandoned delusion, one is liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
One is liberated from suffering, I say.
These, monks, are the two things."
The Sixth.
(AN 2.7, AN 2.1.7, PTS AN i 51) 7. The Discourse on the Dark Side (Kaṇhasutta)
“Bhikkhus, these two things are dark.
Which two?
Moral shamelessness and moral recklessness.”
“Monks, these two things are dark.
This was the seventh [sutta]. (AN 2.8, AN 2.1.8, PTS AN i 51)
8. Sukkasutta “Bhikkhus, these two things are bright.
Which two?
“Moral shame and moral dread.
These, monks, are the two bright qualities.
The eighth.
Cariyāsutta:
“Bhikkhus, these two bright qualities protect the world.”
Which two?
Moral shame and moral dread.

If, monks, these two bright qualities did not protect the world, the concept of "mother," or "maternal aunt," or "uncle's wife," or "teacher's wife," or "the wives of those worthy of respect" would not be known here.
“The world would fall into confusion, like goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, dogs and jackals.
But because, monks, these two bright qualities protect the world, it is recognized as ‘mother’ or ‘aunt’ or ‘maternal uncle’s wife’ or ‘teacher’s wife’ or ‘the wife of one’s elders.
Thus was the ninth [sutta].
Vassūpanāyikasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these two occasions for entering the rains residence. What two? The earlier and the later.”
Which two?
The earlier and the later. These, monks, are the two occasions for entering the rains residence.”
The tenth.
The first chapter on the judicial process.
Its summary verse:
The two exertions are to be praised, the two are to be burned away,
with the fifth being that which has been fully understood;
then there is the fetter and the dark side.
The Chapter on Conduct: With the Rainy-Season Retreat.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.2.
The Chapter on Legal Issues.
“Bhikkhus, there are these two powers. Which two? [The power of wisdom and the power of development. (AN 2.11, AN 2.2.1, PTS AN i 52) “Bhikkhus, there are these two powers. Which two?”
The power of reflection and the power of cultivation.
And what, bhikkhus, is the power of reflection?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person reflects thus:
“Indeed, there is an evil result of bodily misconduct, both in this very life and in future lives;
there is an evil result of verbal misconduct, both in this very life and in future lives; and there is an evil result of mental misconduct, both in this very life and in future lives.”
Having reflected thus, one abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct; one abandons verbal misconduct and develops verbal good conduct;
one abandons mental misconduct and develops mental good conduct; one maintains oneself in purity.
This, monks, is called the power of reflection.
And what, monks, is the power of development?
In this regard, monks, that which is called the power of development is the power of those in training (*śaikṣa*).
For, monks, by relying on that power of one in training, one abandons lust, abandons hatred, and abandons delusion.
“Having abandoned lust, having abandoned hatred, and having abandoned delusion, he does not do what is unwholesome; he does not practice what is evil.
This, monks, is called the power of development.
These, monks, are the two powers.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these two powers. Which two? [The power of reflection and the power of development. (AN 2.12, AN 2.2.2, PTS AN i 52) “Bhikkhus, there are these two powers. Which two?”
The power of reflection and the power of cultivation.
And what, monks, is the power of reflection?
Here, monks, a certain person reflects thus:
‘Indeed, there is an evil result of bodily misconduct, both in this very life and in the future;
there is an evil result of verbal misconduct, both in this very life and in the future; and there is an evil result of mental misconduct, both in this very life and in the future.’
Having reflected thus, one abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct; one abandons verbal misconduct and develops verbal good conduct;
one abandons mental misconduct and develops mental good conduct; one maintains oneself in purity.
This, monks, is called the power of reflection.
And what, bhikkhus, is the power of development?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment;
he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena...
He develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility …

He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
This, monks, is called the power of development.
“These, monks, are the two powers.
(AN 2.13, AN 2.2.3, PTS AN i 53) “Monks,
there are these two powers.
Which two?
The power of reflection and the power of cultivation.
And what, monks, is the power of reflection?
In this case, monks, a certain person reflects thus:
‘The result of bodily misconduct is indeed evil, both in this very life and in the future;
the result of verbal misconduct is indeed evil, both in this very life and in the future; the result of mental misconduct is indeed evil…’
‘The result [of action] occurs both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct;
he abandons verbal misconduct and develops verbal good conduct; he abandons mental misconduct and develops mental good conduct, and he maintains himself in purity.
This, monks, is called the power of reflection.
And what, monks, is the power of development?

Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal serenity and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in happiness who is equanimous and mindful"—thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called the power of development.
These, monks, are the two powers.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these two ways in which the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma. Which two? [The text continues:]”
"In brief and in detail.
These, monks, are the two ways in which the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma.
(AN 2.15, AN 2.2.5, PTS AN i 53)
“Bhikkhus, in whatever legal issue both the bhikkhu who has committed an offense and the bhikkhu who accuses him fail to thoroughly examine themselves,
it can be expected, bhikkhus, that this legal issue will lead to long-term harshness and animosity, and that the bhikkhus will not dwell in comfort.

But in whatever legal issue both the bhikkhu who has committed an offense and the bhikkhu who accuses him do thoroughly examine themselves, it can be expected, bhikkhus, that [the opposite will occur].”
‘It will not lead to long-term harm, suffering, or ruin, and the bhikkhus will dwell in comfort.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu who has committed an offense carefully examine himself?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has committed an offense reflects thus:
‘I have indeed committed an unwholesome act with my body in some respect.
That monk saw me committing an unwholesome act with my body in some respect.
Had I not committed an unwholesome act with my body in some respect, that monk would not have seen me committing an unwholesome act with my body in some respect.’
But because I had committed some unwholesome act with my body, that bhikkhu saw me committing that unwholesome act with my body.
Having seen me committing that unwholesome act with my body, that bhikkhu was displeased.
Being displeased, he spoke words of displeasure to me.
“When I was addressed with words of displeasure by that bhikkhu, I became displeased.
Being displeased, I reported it to others.
Thus, in this matter, a transgression has come upon me alone, just as it would for a customs official regarding the goods.”
"In this way, monks, a monk who has committed an offense carefully examines himself by himself.
And how, monks, does a monk who reproves another carefully examine himself by himself?
Here, monks, a monk who reproves another reflects thus:"
‘This monk, indeed, has committed an unwholesome act with his body in some particular respect.
I saw this monk committing an unwholesome act with his body in some particular respect.
If this monk had not committed an unwholesome act with his body in some particular respect, I would not have seen him committing an unwholesome act with his body in some particular respect.’
But because this bhikkhu has committed an unwholesome act in some respect through his body, therefore I saw this bhikkhu committing an unwholesome act in some respect through his body.
Having seen this bhikkhu committing an unwholesome act in some respect through his body, I was displeased.
Being displeased, I spoke words of displeasure to this bhikkhu.
“When this bhikkhu was addressed by me with words of displeasure, he became displeased.
Being displeased, he reported it to others.
Thus, in this matter, a transgression has overtaken me alone, like that of a tax-collector regarding the goods.”
In this way, monks, the accusing monk thoroughly examines himself by means of himself.
But in whatever legal issue, monks, the monk who has committed an offense and the accusing monk do not thoroughly examine themselves by means of themselves,
in that legal issue, monks, it is to be expected that there will be long-lasting harshness.
"It will lead to harm, and the monks will not dwell in comfort.
But in whatever legal issue, monks, the monk who has committed an offense and the monk who accuses him both carefully examine themselves,
in that legal issue it is to be expected, monks, that there will be no long-term [harm].
"It will lead to roughness and harshness, and the monks will dwell in comfort.
(AN 2.16, AN 2.2.6, PTS AN i 55) Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell?

“Brahmin, it is because of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.”
“What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world?

“It is, brahmin, because of their practice of the Dhamma and practice of the noble life that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!”
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways."
"I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell?”
“It is because of what has been done, brahmin, and because of what has not been done.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, some beings here are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.
“But what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world?”
“Because of what has been done, brahmin, and because of what has not been done.
It is in this way that some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.

“I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by Master Gotama, which has not been explained in detail. May Master Gotama explain it to me in such a way that I may understand the meaning in detail.”

“It would be well if the venerable Gotama would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what the venerable Gotama has spoken in brief without having explained the meaning in detail.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, brahmin, for a certain person, bodily misconduct has been committed and bodily good conduct has not been practiced;
verbal misconduct has been committed and verbal good conduct has not been practiced.”
"Man has committed misconduct of mind, and has not practiced good conduct of mind.

It is in this way, brahmin, through what has been done and what has not been done, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But here, brahmin, some person has practiced good conduct of body, and has not committed misconduct of body..."
“Good verbal conduct has been performed, and bad verbal conduct has not been performed;
good mental conduct has been performed, and bad mental conduct has not been performed.
It is, brahmin, because of what has been done and what has not been done that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”
“Excellent, Master Gotama! … [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
(AN 2.18, AN 2.2.8, PTS AN i 57) Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Ānanda, I declare that misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind are absolutely not to be done.

“Venerable sir, when this misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind—which has been declared by the Blessed One to be absolutely not to be done—is nevertheless committed, what danger is to be expected?
“Ānanda, when this misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind—which has been declared by me to be absolutely not to be done—is committed, this danger is to be expected:”
One reproaches oneself;
the wise, having investigated, censure one;
and an evil reputation spreads abroad.
He dies confused;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell.
Ānanda, this is the danger to be expected when one performs that which I have declared to be absolutely not to be done: namely, bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.”
“Ānanda, I declare that good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind are to be practiced unilaterally.

“Venerable sir, when this good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—which has been declared by the Blessed One as to be practiced unilaterally—is being practiced, what benefit is to be expected?

“Ānanda, when this good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—which has been declared by me as to be practiced unilaterally—is being practiced, this benefit is to be expected:”
One does not reproach oneself;
the wise, having investigated, praise one;
and a good reputation spreads abroad.
He passes away unconfused;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, a heavenly world.

Ānanda, this is the benefit to be expected when that which has been declared by me as an absolute duty—namely, good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—is being performed.”
“Abandon what is unwholesome, monks;
it is possible, monks, to abandon what is unwholesome. (AN 2.19, AN 2.2.9, PTS AN i 58)
“Monks, if it were not possible to abandon the unwholesome, I would not say to you:
‘Monks, abandon the unwholesome.
But because it is possible to abandon the unwholesome, monks, I say this to you.”
“‘Abandon what is unwholesome, bhikkhus,’ I say.
For if the abandoning of what is unwholesome here, bhikkhus, were to lead to harm and suffering, I would not say:
‘Abandon what is unwholesome, bhikkhus.’”
"But because, monks, the abandoning of the unwholesome leads to welfare and happiness, therefore I say to you:
'Monks, abandon the unwholesome.
"Monks, cultivate the wholesome."
"It is possible, monks, to develop what is wholesome.
If it were not possible, monks, to develop what is wholesome, I would not say:
‘Monks, you should develop what is wholesome.’"
But because it is possible, monks, to develop what is wholesome, therefore I say:
"Monks, you should develop what is wholesome.
For if the development of what is wholesome were to lead to harm and suffering, monks, I would not say this.
“‘Cultivate what is wholesome, monks,’ I say.
And because, monks, when the wholesome is cultivated it leads to welfare and happiness, therefore I say:
‘Cultivate what is wholesome, monks.’”
“Monks, these two things lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Which two?
“Both the phrasing and the syllables are poorly set down, and the meaning is poorly explained.
Monks, when the phrasing and syllables are poorly set down, the meaning is also wrongly interpreted.
These, monks, are the two things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Which two?
Well-arranged words and phrases, and well-expounded meaning.”
“Monks, when the words and syllables are well-established, the meaning is also rightly understood.
These, monks, are the two things that lead to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
The second chapter, on legal issues, is concluded.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.21 The Chapter on Fools (Bālavagga) “Monks, there are these two kinds of fools. What two? One who does not know what is beneficial and one who knows it but does not practice it. These, monks, are the two kinds of fools. “There are, monks, these two kinds of wise people. What two? One who knows what is beneficial and one who knows it and practices it. These, monks, are the two kinds of wise people.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of fools. Which two?
One who does not see his transgression as a transgression, and one who does not accept a transgression in accordance with the Dhamma when it is confessed.
"These, monks, are the two kinds of fools.
And these, monks, are the two kinds of wise ones. Which two?"
"One who sees a transgression as a transgression, and one who, when a transgression is confessed, accepts it in accordance with the Dhamma—
these, monks, are the two wise ones.
(AN 2.22, AN 2.3.2, PTS AN i 59)

4. The Chapter on Even-mindedness (Samacittavagga) “Monks,
I will teach you the plane of the true person and the plane of the untrue person.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the plane of the person who is not a true man?
A person who is not a true man, bhikkhus, is ungrateful and unthankful.
For this, bhikkhus, has been declared by the noble ones to be the mark of one who is ungrateful and unthankful: namely, ingratitude and lack of thankfulness.”
“Monks, this is the exclusive domain of the person who is not a true man: namely, ingratitude and a lack of thankfulness.
But, monks, a true man is grateful and thankful.
For this, monks, has been declared by the virtuous: namely, gratitude and thankfulness.”
“Bhikkhus, this alone is the ground of a true person, namely, gratitude and thankfulness.
(AN 2.33, AN 2.4.2, PTS AN i 61) “Bhikkhus,
I say that there are two for whom it is not easy to repay a debt.”
Of which two?
Of mother and father.

Suppose, monks, one were to carry their mother on one shoulder and their father on the other shoulder for a hundred years, living a hundred years, and were to attend to them by anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing them.
And they might even void urine and excrement right there; yet, monks, that would not constitute having done or repaid what is due to one’s mother and father.

And, monks, if one were to establish one’s mother and father as sovereign lords over this great earth abounding in the seven precious treasures, yet, monks, that still would not constitute having done or repaid what is due to one’s mother and father. Why is that?
“Monks, parents are of great service to their children; they are their nurturers, their sustainers, and those who show them this world.
Furthermore, monks, whoever encourages their parents to achieve perfection in faith if they lack faith, establishes them in it, and settles them therein;

encourages them to achieve perfection in virtue if they are immoral, establishes them in it, and settles them therein; and encourages them to achieve perfection in generosity if they are stingy—[that person performs a great deed].”
He settles them [in virtue], establishes them; he encourages, settles, and establishes those lacking wisdom in the perfection of wisdom.
To this extent, monks, parents have both done their duty and repaid their debt.
(AN 2.34, AN 2.4.3, PTS AN i 62)

Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, as he was sitting to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“But in what way, Master Gotama, are you both a proponent of action and a proponent of non-action?
“Brahmin, I speak of non-action regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I speak of the non-performance of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.

“In this way, brahmin, I am both a proponent of action and a proponent of non-action.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said this to the Blessed One:

“Householder, there are two in the world worthy of offerings:
the one in training and the one beyond training.

Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“The learner and the one beyond learning in this world...”
They become worthy of offerings from those who sacrifice;
they are upright in body,
speech, and mind.
That is the field for those who sacrifice;
what is given here bears great fruit.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus.
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"Friends, I will teach you about the person who is fettered internally and the person who is fettered externally.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak."
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“And what, friends, is a person fettered internally?

"Here, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in some order of devas.
Passing away from there, he is a returner, one who comes back to this state of being."
"Friends, this is called a person bound by internal fetters who is a 'returner,' one who comes back to this state of existence.
And what, friends, is a person bound by external fetters?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training."
Thus, having attained and dwelling in a certain peaceful liberation of mind,
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain order of devas.
Passing away from there, he becomes a non-returner, one who does not return to this state of being.
"Friends, this is called a person bound externally who is a non-returner, one who does not come back to this state of being.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous... he trains himself in the training rules he has undertaken.
He practices for the sake of disenchantment with sensual pleasures, for their fading away, and for their cessation."
Thus, you are practicing for disenchantment with existence itself, for dispassion toward it, and for its cessation.
You are practicing for the destruction of craving;
you are practicing for the destruction of greed.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in a certain order of devas.
Passing away from there, he becomes a non-returner, one who does not come back to this state of being.
This, friends, is called a person fettered externally who is a non-returner, one who does not come back to this state of being.

and clinging to sensual lust, and this attachment, fixation, bondage, obsession, preoccupation, and clinging to views.”
“But who, Master Kaccāna, in this world has transcended both this adherence, bondage, obsession, infatuation,
and clinging to sensual lust, and this adherence, bondage, obsession, infatuation, and clinging to views? “There is, brahmin,
a city named Sāvatthī in the eastern provinces.”
Therein dwells the Blessed One at present, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For that Blessed One, brahmin, has transcended this attachment, fixation, bondage, obsession, infatuation, and clinging regarding sensual lust;
and he has transcended this attachment, fixation, bondage, obsession, infatuation, and clinging regarding the lust for views.”

When this was said, the brahmin Ārāmadaṇḍa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, three times uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One!
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One!”
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
For that Blessed One has indeed transcended this attachment, fixation, bondage, obsession, infatuation, and clinging regarding sensual lust;
and he has also transcended this attachment, fixation, bondage, obsession, infatuation, and clinging regarding views.”
“Excellent, Master Kaccāna! Excellent, Master Kaccāna!

Just as, Master Kaccāna, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Kaccāna in many ways.”
"In this very way, Master Kaccāna, the Dhamma has been elucidated by you in many ways.
Venerable Kaccāna, I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
(AN 2.38, AN 2.4.7, PTS AN i 67) On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling at Madhurā in the Gundā Grove.
Then the brahmin Kandarāyana approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he...
Sitting to one side together with the Venerable Mahākaccāna, the brahmin Kandarāyaṇa said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:

“I have heard this, Master Kaccāna: ‘The ascetic Kaccāna does not pay homage to aged brahmins—those who are old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life—nor does he rise up for them, nor does he invite them to a seat.’”
"Is this so, Master Kaccāna?
For Master Kaccāna does not pay homage to, rise up for, or invite with a seat those brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of their life-span.
This, Master Kaccāna, is certainly not proper."
“There is, brahmin, that Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One— who has proclaimed both the stage of the aged and the stage of the young.
Even if, brahmin, one is aged— eighty, ninety, or a hundred years by birth— and yet he indulges in sensual pleasures,
dwells amidst sensual pleasures, is scorched by the fever of sensual pleasures, is consumed by thoughts of sensual pleasure, and is eager for the pursuit of sensual pleasure.”
In that case, that fool does not even count as an elder.
But even if, brahmin, he is young, a youth with beautiful black hair, endowed with the prime of youth and in the first stage of life;

yet he does not indulge in sensual pleasures, he does not dwell in the midst of sensual pleasures, he is not consumed by the fever of sensual pleasures, he is not devoured by thoughts of sensual pleasure, and he is not eager for the pursuit of sensual pleasures.
“Then indeed, that wise man is reckoned as an elder.
When this was said, the brahmin Kandarāyana rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowed his head at the feet of the hundred young bhikkhus, saying:
“Sirs, you are elders; you stand upon the ground of the elders.”
“We are young, standing on the ground of youth.
“Excellent, Master Kaccāna! … [as before] … Let Master Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
(AN 2.39, AN 2.4.8, PTS AN i 68)
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the thieves are powerful, at that time the kings are weak.
On such an occasion, it is not easy for the king to go forth or come back, or to travel through the border regions.
For the brahmins and householders as well, on such an occasion, it is not easy to go forth or come back, or to attend to their external business.”
"In the same way, monks, at whatever time wicked bhikkhus are powerful, at that time well-behaved bhikkhus are weak.
At that time, monks, the well-behaved bhikkhus remain silent, remaining silent as they linger in the midst of the Saṅgha, or they dwell in remote border regions.
This, monks, leads to the harm of many people, to the unhappiness of many people; it is for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including both devas and humans."
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion kings are powerful, on that occasion thieves are weak.
On that occasion it is easy for the king to go forth, to go out, or to travel through the border regions.
On that occasion it is also easy for brahmins and householders to go forth, to go out, or to attend to their external business.”
"In the same way, monks, at whatever time the well-behaved monks are strong, at that time the wicked monks are weak.
At that time, monks, the wicked monks remain silent and withdraw into the midst of the Saṅgha, or they depart elsewhere.
This, monks, leads to the welfare of many, to the happiness of many, to the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including devas and humans."
“Monks, I do not praise wrong practice for two kinds of people: for the householder or for the one gone forth.
Whether it be a householder, monks, or one gone forth, if they practice wrongly, because of that wrong practice, they do not achieve the true way, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.”
“Monks, I praise the right practice of two kinds of persons: either a householder or one who has gone forth.
Whether it be a householder, monks, or one who has gone forth, practicing rightly, by reason of that right practice, they become successful in the true Dhamma that is wholesome.
“Those monks, bhikkhus, who— by means of wrongly grasped discourses that are mere semblances of the letter—
obstruct both the meaning and the Dhamma, are practicing, bhikkhus, for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people,
for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including devas and humans.”
"Monks, those monks produce much demerit and cause the disappearance of this true Dhamma.
But those monks, monks, who— in accordance with the Suttantas well-learned— conform to the meaning and the Dhamma through their semblances of phrasing,
they, monks, have set out for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many."
"For the welfare, benefit, and happiness of people, and for gods and humans alike.
And these bhikkhus, monks, produce much merit; they establish this true Dhamma.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Even-mindedness, is concluded.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.5.1 The Chapter on Assemblies (Parisavagga) “Monks, there are these two assemblies. What two? The assembly that is well-disciplined and the assembly that is not well-disciplined. And what, monks, is the assembly that is not well-disciplined? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus do not train themselves in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction; they do not attend to the Teacher’s teaching; they do not apply themselves to the Teacher’s instruction; they do not practice in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction. This, monks, is called the assembly that is not well-disciplined. And what, monks, is the assembly that is well-disciplined? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus train themselves in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction; they attend to the Teacher’s teaching; they apply themselves to the Teacher’s instruction; they practice in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction. This, monks, is called the assembly that is well-disciplined.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.
Which two?
The shallow assembly and the deep assembly.”
And what, monks, is a shallow assembly?

Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus are restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose-tongued, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, and with unrestrained faculties.
This, monks, is called a shallow assembly.
And what, monks, is a profound assembly? Here, monks,

in whatever assembly the bhikkhus are not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not boisterous, not loose-tongued, but are established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, with one-pointed minds,
and with their sense faculties restrained— this, monks, is called a profound assembly.
"These, monks, are the two assemblies.
Of these two assemblies, monks, the foremost is this: the assembly that is profound.
(AN 2.43, AN 2.5.2, PTS AN i 70)
“Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.
Which two?
The divided assembly and the harmonious assembly.”
And what, monks, is a divided assembly?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus live having fallen into quarreling, strife, and dispute, stabbing one another with the weapons of the tongue.
This, monks, is called a divided assembly.
And what, monks, is a harmonious assembly?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of love.
This, monks, is called a harmonious assembly.
“These, monks, are the two assemblies.
Of these two assemblies, monks, the foremost is the harmonious assembly.
(AN 2.44, AN 2.5.3, PTS AN i 70)
“Monks, there are these two assemblies.
Which two?
The assembly that does not lead by excellence and the assembly that leads by excellence.”
And what, monks, is an assembly that does not lead to the highest?

Here, monks, in whatever assembly the elder bhikkhus are luxurious and indolent, leaders in backsliding, having cast aside the burden of seclusion, and do not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached... [and so forth].
for the realization of what has not yet been realized, for the actualization of what has not yet been actualized.
Subsequent generations follow their example;

they too become luxurious and lax, leaders in falling away, having abandoned the burden of solitude, and they do not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the actualization of what has not yet been actualized.
This, monks, is called an assembly that does not have the foremost.
And what, monks, is an assembly that has the foremost?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the elder bhikkhus are not luxurious, not lax, and do not fall away into decline...
Having laid down their burdens and being pioneers in solitude, they arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained,
for the realization of the unrealized,
and for the actualization of the unactualized. Subsequent generations follow in their footsteps.

She too does not indulge in luxury nor is she lax; she has laid aside the burden of falling away, takes the lead in solitude, and arouses energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, and for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is called the assembly that leads the way.
These, monks, are the two assemblies.
“Bhikkhus, of these two assemblies, this is the foremost: namely, the assembly led by the foremost.
(AN 2.45, AN 2.5.4, PTS AN i 71) “Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.”
Which two?
The assembly of the ignoble and the assembly of the noble.
And what, monks, is the assembly of the ignoble?
In this case, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus do not understand as it really is: “This is suffering”; they do not understand as it really is:
“This is the origin of suffering”; they do not understand as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”;
they do not understand as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
This, monks, is called an ignoble assembly.
And what, monks, is a noble assembly?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus understand, as it truly is, ‘This is suffering.’
“They understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; they understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’;
they understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, monks, is called the noble assembly.”
"These, monks, are the two assemblies.
Of these two assemblies, monks, the foremost is this: the noble assembly.
(AN 2.46, AN 2.5.5, PTS AN i 72)
“Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.
Which two?
The dregs of an assembly and the cream of an assembly.”
"And what, bhikkhus, is a withered assembly?
Here, bhikkhus, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus fall prey to bias through desire, fall prey to bias through hatred, fall prey to bias through delusion, or fall prey to bias through fear.
This, bhikkhus, is called a withered assembly."
And what, monks, is the cream of an assembly?

Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks do not fall into a wrong course through favoritism, nor into a wrong course through hatred, nor into a wrong course through delusion, nor into a wrong course through fear.
This, monks, is called the cream of an assembly.
“These, monks, are the two assemblies.
Of these two assemblies, monks, the foremost is the assembly that is like a cluster of blossoms.
(AN 2.47, AN 2.5.6, PTS AN i 72)
“Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.
Which two?
An assembly trained in concealment but not trained in interrogation, and an assembly trained in interrogation but not trained in concealment.”
And what, monks, is an assembly trained in mere recitation but not trained in inquiry?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus do not wish to listen and do not lend an ear when those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata—
which are profound, profound in meaning, supramundane, and connected with emptiness— are being recited.
They lend an ear, they incline their minds toward understanding, yet they do not consider those teachings as something to be learned or mastered.

However, when those discourses that are poetic, composed in verse, with beautiful phrasing and elegant expression—being external and spoken by disciples—are being recited, they listen intently, lend an ear, and incline their minds toward understanding; they consider those teachings as something to be learned...
They think that [the Dhamma] should be mastered; yet, having mastered that Dhamma, they neither question one another nor investigate it, thinking:
"What is this? What is the meaning of this?"
They do not reveal what has not been revealed, they do not clarify what has not been clarified, and they do not dispel doubt regarding the various matters that give rise to uncertainty.
This, monks, is called an assembly trained in mere recitation, but not trained in interrogation.
And what, monks, is an assembly trained in interrogation, but not trained in mere recitation?

In this case, monks, in whatever assembly monks do not wish to hear, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to understand, and do not consider those discourses— which are poetic, literary, composed with beautiful syllables and phrases, external, and spoken by disciples—
as something to be learned or mastered when they are being recited.
But as for those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata that are profound, of profound meaning, supramundane, and connected with emptiness— when these are being recited,
they listen intently, lend an ear, apply their minds to understanding,
and consider those teachings as something to be mastered and thoroughly learned.
Having mastered that Dhamma, they question one another and investigate it, asking:
"How is this? What is the meaning of this?
They reveal what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been clarified, and dispel doubt regarding various matters that give rise to uncertainty.
“Monks, this is called an assembly trained in cross-examination, not one trained in intimidation.
These, monks, are the two kinds of assemblies.
Of these two, monks, the assembly trained in cross-examination and not trained in intimidation is the foremost.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies. Which two? [The text continues:]”
An assembly that values material things and does not value the true Dhamma; an assembly that values the true Dhamma and does not value material things.
And what, monks, is an assembly that values material things and does not value the true Dhamma?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus speak in praise of one another in the presence of white-robed householders:
‘This monk is one liberated both ways; this one is liberated by wisdom; this one is a body-witness; this one has attained to view;
this one is liberated by faith; this one is a Dhamma-follower; this one is a faith-follower; this one is virtuous and of lovely character;
this one is immoral and of evil character.’
They obtain gain through that.
Having obtained that gain, they enjoy it while being obsessed, infatuated, and clinging to it, without seeing the danger and lacking the wisdom of escape.
This, monks, is called an assembly that values material things, not the true Dharma.
And what, monks, is an assembly that values the true Dhamma and not material gain?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly the bhikkhus do not speak in the presence of white-robed householders in praise of one another, saying:
"Such-and-such a bhikkhu is liberated both ways; such-and-such a bhikkhu is liberated by wisdom; such-and-such a bhikkhu is a body-witness; such-and-such a bhikkhu has attained to view..."
‘This one is liberated by faith; this one is a follower of the Dhamma; this one is a follower by faith; this one is virtuous and of good character;
this one is immoral and of evil character.
Because of that, they obtain gain.

Having obtained those gains, they enjoy them without being tied to them, without being infatuated with them, and without being obsessed by them; seeing the danger in them, they possess the wisdom of escape.
This, monks, is called an assembly that values the true Dhamma, not material things.
These, monks, are the two assemblies.
“Bhikkhus, of these two assemblies, this is the foremost: that which values the true Dhamma, not that which values material things.
(AN 2.49, AN 2.5.8, PTS AN i 74) “Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.”
Which two?
An uneven assembly and an even assembly. And what, monks, is an uneven assembly?

In this case, monks, in whatever assembly unlawful proceedings are carried out and lawful proceedings are not carried out; unlawful proceedings are illuminated and lawful proceedings are not illuminated;

unlawful proceedings shine forth and lawful proceedings do not shine forth; and non-disciplinary proceedings are carried out and disciplinary proceedings are not carried out; non-disciplinary proceedings are illuminated and disciplinary proceedings are not illuminated.
This, monks, is called an uneven assembly.
(…) And what, monks, is an even assembly?
Here, monks, in whatever assembly formal acts according to the Dhamma are carried out, and formal acts contrary to the Dhamma are not carried out—this, monks, is called an even assembly.
Disciplinary acts proceed, while non-disciplinary acts do not proceed; lawful acts shine forth, while unlawful acts do not shine forth;
disciplinary acts shine forth, while non-disciplinary acts do not shine forth.
This, monks, is called a harmonious assembly. (…)
"These, monks, are the two assemblies.
Of these two assemblies, monks, the foremost is this: the assembly that is harmonious.
(AN 2.50, AN 2.5.9, PTS AN i 75)
“Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies.
Which two?
The assembly that is unrighteous and the assembly that is righteous... These, bhikkhus, are the two assemblies.”
“Monks, of these two assemblies, this is the foremost: namely, the assembly that is righteous.

6. Chapter on Persons (Puggalavagga) “Monks,
these two persons, appearing in the world, appear for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.”
Which two?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Wheel-turning Monarch.
